slides.title: Cognitive science: the science of mind
slides.body:
**Cognitive science**: interdisciplinary study of mind + intelligence. Five core fields: psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, computer science (CS+AI). Foundational period 1950s-60s with cognitive revolution overturning behaviorism. Marr's three levels of analysis (1982): computational (what + why); algorithmic (how processed); implementational (physical substrate).

**Key methods**: behavioral experiments (RT + accuracy); psychophysics (just-noticeable differences, signal detection theory); neuroimaging (EEG, MEG, fMRI, TMS, ECoG, single-unit); computational modeling (ACT-R, neural networks, Bayesian, RL); brain stimulation; lesion studies.

**Recent revolutions**: deep learning + neural network models (~2012-); Bayesian cognitive science (Tenenbaum + others 2000s); active inference + predictive processing (Friston 2010s); large-language-model-based cognitive models (2020s).

slides.title: Visual hierarchy + the ventral + dorsal streams
slides.body:
**Visual processing**: retina → LGN (thalamus) → V1 → V2 → V4 → IT (ventral 'what' stream) + MT/MST → parietal (dorsal 'where/how' stream). Hierarchical processing.

**Receptive-field properties**:
- Retinal ganglion cells: center-surround.
- V1 simple cells: oriented edges (Hubel + Wiesel Nobel 1981).
- V1 complex cells: oriented edges + position-invariance.
- V2 + V4: more complex (contours, color, texture).
- IT: object selectivity (face cells, place cells, body cells).
- FFA (fusiform face area; Kanwisher 1997): face-selective.
- PPA (parahippocampal place area): scene-selective.

**Two streams (Ungerleider + Mishkin 1982)**:
- **Ventral 'what'**: object identification + recognition.
- **Dorsal 'where' or 'how'**: spatial location + action guidance.
- Patients with damage dissociate: ventral lesion → agnosia; dorsal → optic ataxia.

**Deep neural networks (DNNs) + visual cortex**: AlexNet 2012 + later showed striking match between DNN feature hierarchy + ventral stream. Yamins + DiCarlo 2014: CNN units predict V4 + IT neuron responses. Modern: foundation models match cortex even better.

slides.title: Bayesian perception + prediction
slides.body:
**Bayesian perception** (Helmholtz 1860s; Geisler 2003+; Tenenbaum + Yuille; Friston): perception is unconscious inference combining sensory likelihood + prior expectations:

  P(world | sensory) ∝ P(sensory | world) × P(world)

Explains: optical illusions (priors override sensory); shape-from-shading; depth perception; multi-sensory integration (Ernst + Banks 2002 MLE).

**Predictive processing / active inference** (Friston 2010s, Clark 2013): brain is a 'prediction machine.' Top-down predictions about sensory inputs; bottom-up prediction errors update beliefs. Minimize free energy = prediction-error surprise.

**Hierarchical Bayesian models**: cortical hierarchy implements iterative belief-updating. Each level predicts next; prediction errors propagate up.

**Examples + applications**:
- Hollow-mask illusion: prior for convex faces overrides depth cues.
- Cocktail party problem: priors aid selection.
- Hallucinations: aberrant priors (predictive-coding theory of schizophrenia).
- Autism: weak priors → overdependence on bottom-up sensory.
- Modern: large-language + multimodal models as Bayesian predictors.

question.question: Apply Bayesian inference to a perceptual task
question.goal: You see a tree silhouette in dim light. Compute posterior probability it's a person.

steps.prompt: Prior P(person at this location, time, context)?
steps.reveal: P(person) ≈ 0.001 (1/1000) in remote area; higher in urban setting.

steps.prompt: P(tree at location) ≈ 0.999 (in remote area). Posterior P(person | silhouette)?
steps.reveal: P(person | silhouette) = 0.7×0.001 / (0.7×0.001 + 0.3×0.999) ≈ 0.0023 ≈ 0.23%. Despite strong likelihood match, low prior dominates → silhouette likely a tree. Captures human perceptual inference: priors heavily influence interpretation. Same data + different priors → different perceptions (e.g., bear vs rock at dusk).

question.question: Match each region/area to its functional specialization.
question.explanation: Cortical visual + cognitive specialization: V1-V2 early features; IT/FFA object/face identity; MT/parietal motion + action; PFC decision + control. Hierarchy + parallel streams established by lesion studies, single-unit recordings, fMRI, modern decoding methods.

question.question: Why do deep neural networks (DNNs) match visual-cortex responses so closely?
options: DNNs trained on object-recognition tasks (ImageNet, etc.) learn hierarchical feature representations (edges → textures → parts → objects) similar to what evolution + experience built in visual cortex. Yamins + DiCarlo 2014, Khaligh-Razavi + Kriegeskorte: CNN units predict V4 + IT neuron firing better than any other model. Suggests: (1) object recognition is the dominant computational task; (2) hierarchical feature learning is the natural solution; (3) DNNs are useful models of cortical computation. Modern: foundation models + brain-aligned objectives.
question.explanation: DNNs trained on object recognition learn hierarchical features that match cortical responses. Yamins + DiCarlo 2014 (V4 + IT prediction); Khaligh-Razavi 2014; many follow-ups. Provides: model of cortical computation; predictions for new stimuli; bridge between psychology + neuroscience + ML. Limitations: DNNs differ in some details (texture bias, adversarial examples). Modern: brain-aligned objectives, vision-language models, ANNs as theory.

slides.workedSolution: DNNs (Yamins + DiCarlo 2014) trained on object recognition (ImageNet) learn hierarchical features matching V1 → V4 → IT cortex; predict neuron firing better than other models. Suggests object recognition is dominant evolutionary task + hierarchical learning natural solution. ANN-as-theory framework: DNNs as cortical models.

question.question: Drag to the approximate retinal ganglion cell count per eye (in millions).
question.explanation: Each retina: ~1-1.5 million ganglion cells. Each carries info to brain via optic nerve. Compares: ~100 million rods + 5 million cones in retina (compressed); ~100 billion neurons total in brain.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why optical illusions reveal important truths about visual perception.
question.rubric: Mentions: optical illusions exploit assumptions/priors brain uses to interpret ambiguous sensory input. Examples: Müller-Lyer (length depends on context arrows; 3D-depth-inference priors); Necker cube (bistable percept; brain picks one interpretation); checker-shadow (lightness constancy via illumination priors); hollow-mask (convex-face prior overrides depth cues). Reveal: perception is constructive + inferential, not passive recording; priors shape what we see; ambiguities resolved via Bayesian-like inference. Modern: predictive-processing framework (Friston, Clark) explains illusions as prediction-error minimization under priors. Implications for neuroscience (hierarchical generative models); psychiatry (aberrant priors in hallucinations); ML (vision models). Concludes: illusions are not perceptual failures but features of efficient inference that usually works.
